title: Profit from stocks: capital gains and dividends
subtitle: Making money from stocks
openingQuestion: You buy HPG (Hoa Phat) shares at VND 25,000, a year later the price rises to VND 30,000 and the company also pays a cash dividend of VND 1,000/share. What two sources is your profit coming from?
openingOptions: From capital gains (buy-sell price difference) and from dividends - two independent sources of stock return
From the interest rate set by the state bank, added on top of the share's value every year
Only from reselling the stock at a higher price than the original purchase price, no other source
Only from the cash dividend the company decides to pay shareholders, unrelated to the share price
explanation: Profit from a stock comes from two sources: the price gain when sold and the dividends received while holding. Counting only one of the two is a common mistake - comparing two investments by price alone ignores the entire dividend received. It's also important to distinguish cash dividends from stock dividends: the latter only slices the same old pie into more pieces, without bringing you any additional money.

diagram.label: Buy a stock at some price
Pays part as dividends, keeps the rest for growth
Sell: the price gain is capital gain - add both for the real return

realWorldExample.description: Vinamilk is one of the most consistent cash-dividend payers on HOSE, maintaining a VND 4,000-4,500/share/year dividend for many years. An investor holding 1,000 VNM shares can receive several million VND in cash dividends each year, plus potential capital gains if the share price rises over time - even though VNM is a slower-growing company than tech or real-estate companies.

quiz.question: Why do some fast-growing companies (like emerging tech companies) usually not pay dividends, or pay very little?
options: Because the company retains profit to reinvest
Because most shareholders proactively refuse to accept dividends
Because most emerging tech companies are running at a loss
Because the law bans tech companies from paying dividends to shareholders
quiz.explanation: Many high-growth companies prioritize keeping retained earnings to invest in expansion instead of paying dividends, expecting that reinvestment will create greater company value, reflected as capital gains (a rising share price) in the long run.

quiz.question: If you buy a stock at VND 50,000 and after 2 years the price falls to VND 40,000, even though the company still pays dividends regularly, what does this mean?
options: A falling share price has no effect at all on the total actual profit you receive from the investment
You could still be running a net loss if the capital loss (VND 10,000/share) exceeds the total dividends received over the 2 years
The dividends received are always enough to fully offset any decline in price, no matter how large the drop is no matter how small that loss turns out to be
You're definitely in profit simply because you received regular dividends over the 2-year holding period
quiz.explanation: Total return from a stock = capital gain/loss + dividends received. If the price falls VND 10,000/share but you only receive, say, VND 3,000 in dividends over 2 years, you're still running a net loss of VND 7,000/share as of that point (before selling).

quiz.question: How does a stock dividend differ from a cash dividend?
options: Stock dividends are only for large shareholders, cash dividends for small ones
Stock dividends are paid earlier, cash dividends paid at the end of the following year which is the whole point of the mechanism
Stock dividends increase the number of shares you hold, without putting money in your pocket
Stock dividends aren't taxed while cash dividends are
quiz.explanation: A cash dividend is real money transferred into your account. A stock dividend just slices the same pie: you have more shares, but the price per share is adjusted down proportionally, so the value of your holding at that moment doesn't change.

quiz.question: Company A pays a dividend of VND 2,000 per share on a stock trading at VND 40,000. What is the dividend yield?
options: Cannot be calculated without knowing the company's profit
quiz.explanation: Dividend yield = annual dividend divided by share price = 2,000 / 40,000 = 5%. This figure lets you compare directly against a savings interest rate - but unlike savings, the share price can fall, and the company can cut the dividend in any year.

quiz.question: Why does a share price typically fall right on the ex-dividend date?
options: Because the money about to leave the company reduces the value of each share proportionally
Because the exchange temporarily halts matching so the price gets adjusted down reflecting money that has actually left the company
Because investors all sell off right after receiving the dividend
Because the company issues new shares to fund the dividend payment
quiz.explanation: Dividend money leaves the company's assets, so from the ex-dividend session, new buyers no longer get that payment - the reference price is therefore adjusted down by exactly the dividend amount. This isn't a loss: existing shareholders receive that exact difference in cash instead.

quiz.question: One stock pays a very high, steady dividend, while another pays none at all. Which is better?
options: The high-dividend stock, since cash in hand is always more certain than an expectation
It depends on how well the company uses retained earnings
The one that pays no dividend, since the company is reinvesting so it will grow fast
The high-dividend stock, since that proves the company can't possibly lose money
quiz.explanation: Dividends don't automatically make you richer - it's money moved from the company to your pocket, and the share price falls correspondingly. The real question is: if retained, would the company generate more than that amount? For a company with good expansion opportunities left, retaining is right; for a mature company, paying out is right.

keyTakeaways: Stocks generate return through two independent channels: capital gain (buy-sell price difference) and dividends (direct profit sharing)
Fast-growing companies usually prioritize reinvestment over dividends; stable companies (like Vinamilk) usually pay dividends regularly
Real return must be calculated by summing both channels, not looking at price alone or dividends alone

practicePrompt.question: You buy stock X at VND 80,000, receiving a total of VND 4,000/share in dividends over 2 years. The share price is now VND 70,000. As of now, is your investment in profit or loss?
options: In a net loss of about VND 6,000/share, since the VND 10,000 capital loss exceeds the VND 4,000 total dividends received
In net profit because you received regular dividends over the 2 years, regardless of how much the price has fallen from purchase
Exactly breaking even, since dividends received are always designed to offset exactly the amount the price has fallen
Cannot be determined, since profit from a stock is only calculated from the final sale price, unrelated to dividends
practicePrompt.explanation: Capital loss: 80,000 - 70,000 = VND 10,000/share. Dividends received: VND 4,000/share. Net loss = 10,000 - 4,000 = VND 6,000/share. Both return channels must be added together to correctly assess the investment result.

summary.keyIdea: Stocks generate return through two independent channels: capital gain (buy-sell price difference) and dividends (direct profit sharing)
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Fast-growing companies usually prioritize reinvestment over dividends; stable companies (like Vinamilk) usually pay dividends regularly

application.title: Separate capital gain from dividends
application.message: Pick a stock you know, look up its 1-year price history and dividend-payment history, then add the two amounts yourself to estimate the investor's actual total return.
application.secondary: Many people only look at the price and forget to add dividends - this calculation will reveal that gap.

sections.text: When someone says 'I made money on this stock', they could be talking about one of two very different things: the price went up, or the dividends received. Understanding these two sources of return helps you correctly assess a stock investment, instead of just looking at the price on the ticker.
Capital gain: the difference between buy and sell price

This is the most intuitive source of profit. You buy a stock at one price, then sell at a higher price, and that difference is the capital gain. For example, buying HPG at VND 25,000 and selling at VND 30,000 gives a capital gain of VND 5,000/share, equal to 20% on original capital - before fees and tax.

Capital gain only becomes real money once you sell the stock. Before that, no matter how much the price has risen, it's still just an 'unrealized gain' - which can disappear if the price reverses before you manage to sell.
Dividends: the share of profit the company pays directly

A dividend is the after-tax profit a company decides to pay back to shareholders, instead of keeping all of it for reinvestment. Dividends can be paid in cash (transferred straight into your securities account) or as bonus shares (you receive more shares instead of cash).

items: Cash dividend: the company transfers money directly, e.g. VND 2,000/share - if you hold 1,000 shares, you receive VND 2 million
Stock dividend: the company issues additional shares to existing shareholders proportionally, e.g. 10% means holding 1,000 shares gets you 100 more
Dividend yield = dividend per share divided by current share price - lets you compare how attractive dividends are across companies
Not every company pays dividends regularly - the decision depends on strategy and financial condition each year

sections.label: Why growth companies usually pay fewer dividends
sections.text: Companies like emerging tech companies or fast-expanding companies usually retain almost all of their profit to reinvest - building new plants, hiring more staff, developing products. Shareholders accept receiving no dividend because they expect the company's value (and share price) to grow much faster than the small dividends they might otherwise receive.
Calculating total return: don't look at only half the picture

The real total return from a stock investment must add both: (sale price minus purchase price) plus total dividends received throughout the holding period. Many beginners only watch the price fall and panic-sell, forgetting that the dividends received during that time are also a real part of the return.

lines: Stocks generate return through two channels: capital gain when the price rises, and dividends when the company shares profit.
Assessing a stock investment requires looking at the total of both, not just price movement on the ticker.
